prompt: English has become the main language of international business, science and travel. Some people see this as a practical advantage, while others believe it threatens smaller languages and the cultures attached to them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
It is worth noticing which languages have actually disappeared over the past century, because the answer complicates the usual story. Very few were replaced by English. They were replaced by the national language of the state they happened to fall inside — by Mandarin, Spanish, Russian, Bahasa Indonesia — through school systems, broadcasting and the requirement that official business be conducted in one tongue. English is the most visible language in the world, but rarely the one doing the killing.

That the shared language is convenient is not in dispute. A Brazilian engineer and a Korean supplier can settle a specification in an afternoon rather than a month; a doctor in one country can read a trial published in another without waiting years for a translation. Whatever else globalisation has produced, this is a straightforward gain, and the alternative is not a fairer multilingualism but a slower and more expensive version of the same exchange, mediated by whoever can afford interpreters.

The danger the second view identifies is nevertheless real, though it works through incentives rather than through any prohibition. No government forbids a minority language; parents make an entirely rational calculation about their children's prospects and stop transmitting one. Within two generations a language can retreat from the kitchen to the funeral, and what goes with it is not sentimental. Systems for classifying plants, tides, weather and kinship, refined over centuries and never written down, exist only in the speech of the last generation to use them daily.

So both views are correct, but the second is aimed slightly off target. Attacking English would not save a single endangered language, because the pressure comes from the language of their own capital city, not from Washington or London. What would help is unglamorous and expensive: minority-language schooling, broadcasting and administration substantial enough that a parent choosing that language is not choosing a disadvantage for their child. English can remain the world's second language without any of this being lost — but only if someone pays for the first one.
title: English as a world language
